method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)' (published online 14 May 2021), 24 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 ('This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License'); © The Author(s) 2021 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC8816529). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055) 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients' (published 5 October 2016), 11 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (© 2016 The authors) (read at PMC JATS XML <license> element for PMC5314807 (copy fetched in Wave 6, src/para/hypercalcaemia_sfe.xml)). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. S1 was chosen because it is the only open source found that supports the PBS row's items (calcitonin, a low-calcium diet, phosphate supplementation). Edition 2.0 adds S2, the Society for Endocrinology adult emergency guidance (Endocr Connect 2016, PMC5314807, CC BY-NC-ND), to cover adults; it was set aside in Wave 6 because it does not support those PBS items, but it is a society guideline for the same condition. Its box-format text survived extraction (0 tables stripped). S2 is paraphrased and hash-anchored; all S1 claims are unchanged.

claims.claim: **Infant hypercalcaemia is uncommon but can cause lasting harm:** nephrocalcinosis with permanent kidney damage, osteoporosis and neurodevelopmental impairment.
claims.source_text: Hypercalcaemia in the neonate and infant, although uncommon, can have serious long-term consequences, including nephrocalcinosis that may cause permanent kidney damage, osteoporosis and neurodevelopmental impairments
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hypercalcaemia means a serum calcium more than two standard deviations above the normal mean; use age-appropriate ranges,** because calcium runs higher in newborns and preterm infants.
claims.source_text: Hypercalcaemia is defined as a serum calcium concentration two standard deviations greater than the normal mean. An accurate determination of the serum calcium concentration with age-appropriate normal ranges (Table 2) is required as serum calcium levels are higher in newborns and preterm infants and decline with age
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look for failure to thrive, poor feeding, constipation, polyuria, irritability, lethargy, seizures and hypotonia.**
claims.source_text: Hypercalcaemia presents clinically with a range of symptoms including failure to thrive, poor feeding, constipation, polyuria, irritability, lethargy, seizures and hypotonia.
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Work-up:** family and diet history; examination for dysmorphic features, granulomatous disease or subcutaneous fat deposits; total and ionised calcium, albumin, phosphate, creatinine, intact PTH, vitamin D metabolites, and urine calcium, phosphate and creatinine.
claims.source_text: When hypercalcaemia is suspected, an accurate diagnosis will require an evaluation of potential causes (e.g. family history or diet) and assessment for physical features (such as dysmorphology, granulomatous disease or subcutaneous fat deposits), as well as biochemical measurements. These measurements should include total and ionised serum calcium, serum albumin to calculate corrected serum calcium, serum phosphate, creatinine, intact PTH, vitamin D metabolites and urinary calcium, phosphate and creatinine
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Sort the cause by PTH:** neonatal causes are maternal or neonatal and split into high-PTH and low-PTH disorders.
claims.source_text: Neonatal hypercalcaemia can be due to maternal or neonatal factors and can be divided into high or low PTH disorders
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Transient neonatal hypercalcaemia from maternal hypocalcaemia** is usually diagnosed by checking the mother's calcium and the family history, and usually settles within a few weeks.
claims.source_text: In most cases, measuring maternal serum calcium and determining whether a familial or maternal history of hypercalcaemia exists are sufficient for diagnosis. The hypercalcaemia in the neonate is usually resolved within a few weeks
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other causes to consider:** thyroid disease (hyper- or hypothyroidism), adrenal insufficiency, and medicines such as thiazides and lithium.
claims.source_text: Hypercalcaemia may occur in association with a number of endocrine disorders including hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency … including medications (such as thiazides and lithium)
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism usually presents in the first 2 weeks with calcium above 4.5 mmol/L and can be fatal if untreated.**
claims.source_text: Individuals with NSHPT usually present within the first 2 weeks post-partum with serum calcium levels of > 4.5 mmol/L … can be fatal if untreated
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Early parathyroidectomy is the preferred treatment,** with bisphosphonates to bring calcium down beforehand; cinacalcet has lowered PTH and calcium in some infants, but its effect depends on genotype.
claims.source_text: Parathyroidectomy is the preferred treatment for NSHPT, with bisphosphonates used to reduce hypercalcaemia prior to surgery []. Surgery should be performed early to avoid neuromotor restrictions, which may persist after otherwise successful surgery, and has been correlated with microcephaly and the duration or amplitude of hypercalcaemia []. The CaSR-positive allosteric modulator, cinacalcet, which enhances receptor sensitivity to extracellular calcium, has successfully reduced PTH and serum calcium in some NSHPT patients [, ]. The efficacy of cinacalcet is genotype dependent and may be ineffective in some patients
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is usually benign and persists after parathyroidectomy,** so distinguish it from primary hyperparathyroidism (genetics, urine calcium/creatinine ratio below 0.02) to avoid needless surgery.
claims.source_text: FHH1 is usually benign, and although its biochemical features have considerable overlap with typical primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT), hypercalcaemia in FHH remains persistent following parathyroidectomy. It is therefore important to distinguish between typical PHPT and FHH to avoid unnecessary surgery [, ]. This should involve a combination of genetic analysis, measurement of urinary calcium/creatinine ratio (UCCR) (cut-off of < 0.02 for FHH1)
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cinacalcet for symptomatic FHH has been reported in children, but its safety and efficacy there are unproven** and it is not FDA-approved for this age group.
claims.source_text: Treatment of symptomatic hypercalcaemia with cinacalcet has been reported in some adults and young children with FHH1 [, ]. However, the safety and efficacy have not been thoroughly examined in children, and the FDA has not approved its use in this age group
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Nutritional causes:** excess calcium in enriched formulas, or too little dietary phosphate, can raise calcium.
claims.source_text: Hypercalcaemia can occur in the neonate or young infant following ingestion of excess calcium in enriched formulas. Low dietary phosphate can also cause hypercalcaemia, due to suppression of FGF23 or elevations in 1,25(OH)2D3.
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In formula- or parenterally-fed preterm infants, equimolar calcium:phosphate ratios (0.75:1 to 1:1) and close electrolyte and phosphorus monitoring are advised;** changing formula and/or giving phosphate supplements corrected hypophosphataemia.
claims.source_text: formulas with equimolar (0.75:1 to 1:1) Ca2+:PO4 ratios, along with careful monitoring of electrolytes including phosphorus have been recommended to prevent hypercalcaemia and hypophosphatemia [, ]. Hypophosphatemia has been described in some infants given correctly prepared formulas, and it has been suggested that bioavailability of phosphorus may be suboptimal in some infants in the context of gastrointestinal disease or tube feeding []. Formula change and/or phosphate supplementation improved hypophosphatemia in these infants
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Vitamin D excess (in the infant or the breastfeeding mother):** rehydration with furosemide usually fixes it; bisphosphonates have been used when 25(OH)D stayed high.
claims.source_text: Excessive vitamin D intake, either by the infant or the breast-feeding mother can lead to increased intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, enhanced bone resorption, and consequently hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphatemia []. Rehydration therapy with furosemide usually resolves hypercalcaemia in these infants, although bisphosphonates have been used in patients in which 25(OH)D remained high
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia (IIH) presents in the first year** with suppressed PTH, hypercalciuria and often nephrocalcinosis; calcium usually normalises before age three, but nephrocalcinosis and hypercalciuria may persist, and early diagnosis limits kidney damage.
claims.source_text: IIH classically presents in the first year of life with typical symptoms of hypercalcaemia, including failure to thrive, weight loss, dehydration, polyuria, vomiting and lethargy []. Hypercalcaemia results from intestinal hyperabsorption [] and is accompanied by suppressed intact PTH and hypercalciuria []. Nephrocalcinosis is also observed on kidney ultrasonography in infants from a few months of age []. Hypercalcaemia generally resolves before the age of three years, although nephrocalcinosis and persistent hypercalciuria can continue to be common []. If diagnosed early, the prognosis of IIH patients can be improved, and extent of nephrocalcinosis limited
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IIH with SLC34A1 variants (2016) adds hypophosphataemia from kidney phosphate wasting** to the classic picture.
claims.source_text: In 2016, mutations in a second gene, SLC34A1, which encodes the kidney proximal tubule sodium-phosphate co-transporter NaPi-IIa, were identified in patients with IIH []. Again, these mutations were autosomal recessive and led to inactivation of the NaPi-IIa protein []. This subset of patients not only have the classical symptoms of hypercalcaemia and suppressed PTH but also exhibit hypophosphatemia due to kidney phosphate wasting
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In Williams syndrome, hypercalcaemia is reported in 5% to 50%;** it usually resolves in the first few years but may return at puberty.
claims.source_text: There are discrepancies in the reported frequency of hypercalcaemia in association with Williams syndrome, ranging from as low as 5% to up to 50% [, ]. The high serum calcium levels are usually resolved within the first few years but may recur during puberty
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn** (weeks after a traumatic birth or therapeutic hypothermia) can cause fatal hypercalcaemia; it responds to furosemide and glucocorticoids, and bisphosphonates normalised calcium with less recurrence.
claims.source_text: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn is another rare cause of hypercalcaemia that normally arises within a few weeks of birth … Although subcutaneous fat necrosis usually self-resolves, the associated hypercalcaemia, caused by a combination of calcium release from necrotic tissue and excess calcitriol and prostaglandin E activity from the granulomatous reaction, can be fatal []. Hypercalcaemia associated with subcutaneous fat necrosis has been shown to respond to furosemide and glucocorticoid treatment, although an increased incidence of nephrocalcinosis may occur in these infants. Bisphosphonate treatment successfully resolved serum calcium levels and had a reduced risk of recurrent hypercalcaemia
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **In every case, stop vitamin D supplements at once and rehydrate;** rehydration with furosemide often works in Williams syndrome, though some children need more.
claims.source_text: Vitamin D supplementation must be stopped immediately in all cases and rehydration performed. Rehydration therapy combined with furosemide is often successful in reducing serum calcium in patients with Williams syndrome; however, some children are unresponsive and require further treatment
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bisphosphonates have been used in Williams syndrome** with normal calcium afterwards and no adverse effects reported.
claims.source_text: Bisphosphonates have been used to treat hypercalcaemia in several cases of Williams syndrome [, ]. Serum calcium levels remained normal in these infants and adverse effects were not observed
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **A low-calcium diet works in IIH and Williams syndrome but needs close monitoring,** because it can cause calcium deficiency and rickets, and it may not fully normalise calcium and PTH.
claims.source_text: A number of studies have demonstrated a low calcium diet is effective in treating hypercalcaemia in IIH and Williams syndrome, although this must be closely monitored due to its potential to induce calcium deficiency and rickets [, ]. Moreover, low calcium diet may not successfully normalise serum calcium and PTH levels
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Corticosteroids are often used for symptomatic hypercalcaemia but should be brief,** and in CYP24A1 disease they sometimes fail.
claims.source_text: Often, corticosteroids are used for the treatment of symptomatic hypercalcaemia as they can inhibit enteral calcium absorption and induce CYP24A1 expression []. However, a study of adults with CYP24A1 mutations showed corticosteroids fail to lower serum calcium levels, normalise PTH levels and decrease urinary calcium excretion in some individuals []. Use of corticosteroids should be short to avoid their well-documented side effects
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Calcitonin has worked (alongside thiazides for hypercalciuria), but tachyphylaxis within 48 h limits it to short-term use.**
claims.source_text: Descriptions of the successful use of calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclastic bone resorption and enhances kidney calcium excretion, have also been described to treat hypercalcaemia, in combination with thiazide diuretics to reduce hypercalciuria []. However, repeated administration of calcitonin leads to tachyphylaxis within 48 h, limiting its long-term use
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cellulose phosphate, which binds dietary calcium, has resolved IIH hypercalcaemia** but is unavailable in some countries.
claims.source_text: The administration of cellulose phosphate, which binds calcium with high affinity thereby inhibiting intestinal absorption, has also been described to successfully resolve hypercalcaemia in IIH, although this treatment is not available in some countries
claims.locator: Gorvin CM, et al. Pediatric Nephrology 37(2), Springer; doi:10.1007/s00467-021-05082-z, 'Genetic causes of neonatal and infantile hypercalcaemia (educational review)', published online 14 May 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8816529/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Grade by albumin-adjusted calcium:** below 3.0 mmol/L is often symptom-free and usually needs no urgent correction; 3.0–3.5 may be tolerated if it rose slowly but usually warrants prompt treatment; above 3.5 needs urgent correction because of the risk of arrhythmia and coma.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Features to look for:** thirst and polyuria; anorexia, nausea and constipation; low mood, cognitive change, confusion or coma; renal impairment; a short QT and arrhythmias; kidney stones or nephrocalcinosis; pancreatitis; peptic ulcer; hypertension or cardiomyopathy; muscle weakness; band keratopathy.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Causes:** primary hyperparathyroidism or cancer account for ninety percent. Rarer causes include thiazides, familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, granulomatous disease, thyrotoxicosis, tertiary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D or A excess, lithium, immobilisation, adrenal insufficiency, milk-alkali syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, theophylline toxicity and phaeochromocytoma.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Assess:** how long symptoms have been present, clues to a cause (weight loss, night sweats, cough), family history and all medicines including supplements and over-the-counter products; examine cognition, fluid status and neck, chest, abdomen, breasts and lymph nodes; do an ECG for a short QT; send adjusted calcium, phosphate, PTH, urea and electrolytes.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Read the PTH:** high calcium with high PTH means primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism; with low PTH, think malignancy or a rarer cause. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia can look like primary hyperparathyroidism, but it is rarely severe or an emergency.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Rehydrate first: IV 0.9% saline, 4–6 L over 24 h,** watching for fluid overload in the elderly or with renal impairment; severe renal failure may need dialysis.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Loop diuretics are seldom used in adults** (S2): only if fluid overload develops, since they do not lower calcium effectively.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **If saline is not enough, give an IV bisphosphonate:** a 15-minute infusion of zoledronic acid 4 mg; ibandronic acid 2–4 mg; or pamidronate 30–90 mg, chosen by severity, infused at 20 mg/h. Infuse more slowly and consider a lower dose in renal impairment. Calcium bottoms out at 2–4 days; hypocalcaemia can follow if vitamin D is low or PTH is suppressed.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Second line: glucocorticoids (they reduce 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production)** for lymphoma, other granulomatous disease or 25-hydroxyvitamin D poisoning: prednisolone 40 mg daily, usually working within 2–4 days.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Calcimimetics, denosumab and calcitonin are specialist options** when the response to other measures is poor.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Parathyroidectomy** can be considered when primary hyperparathyroidism presents acutely with severe hypercalcaemia that responds poorly to other treatment.
claims.locator: Walsh J, Gittoes N, Selby P, for the Society for Endocrinology Clinical Committee, Endocrine Connections 5(5):G9 (doi 10.1530/EC-16-0055), 'Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients', published 5 October 2016, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5314807/, retrieved 2026-09-24
